pedagogy.summary: Money and measure problems weave fractions and decimals together in context: finding a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 = 80p), subtracting decimal measures (2.5 − 0.75 = 1.75 m), and moving between fractions, decimals and units (3/10 of 1 kg = 300 g = 0.3 kg). Success rests on reading a decimal by its place value rather than as two whole numbers, keeping units consistent, and choosing whether a fraction-of or a decimal calculation is easiest.
bestPractices: Read money by place value: £3.20 is 3 pounds and 2 tenths of a pound = 20p, NOT '3 pounds 2 pence'
Equalise decimal lengths and align the point before subtracting (2.50 − 0.75)
Connect a fraction of an amount to division: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p
Convert between units deliberately and both ways (0.3 kg = 300 g; 300 g = 0.3 kg)
Estimate first to sense-check the size of the answer
keyRepresentations: Bar model partitioned for a fraction of an amount
Place-value columns aligned on the decimal point
Number line / ruler for the rope-length problem
kg↔g (or £↔p) double number line for unit conversion
commonMisconceptions: Reads money as two whole numbers: '£3.20 = 3 pounds 2 pence', '£3.5 = 3 pounds 5 pence'
Misaligns decimals of unequal length when subtracting (2.5 − 0.75)
Miscomputes a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 ≠ 80p)
Unit slips: 0.3 kg read as 30 g or 3000 g, or gives grams but not the decimal of a kg

learn.summary: Children solve money and measure problems that weave fractions and decimals together: finding a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 = 80p), subtracting decimal measures of unequal length (2.5 − 0.75 = 1.75 m), and moving between fractions, decimals and units (3/10 of 1 kg = 300 g = 0.3 kg). Success rests on reading each decimal digit by its place value rather than as two separate whole numbers, keeping units consistent, aligning on the decimal point before subtracting, and connecting 'a fraction of' to division.

activities.title: Split the £3.20 bar: a quarter as division
feedback: If a part reads 8p or 12.8p, check: do the four equal parts add back to £3.20? 80p × 4 = £3.20, so each quarter is 80p.
The 12.8p trap treats £3.20 as the bare number 3.2 and multiplies (3.2 × 4 = 12.8) instead of dividing; 'a quarter OF' makes the amount smaller, so you divide.
If 'a quarter' was treated as 25 of something, connect ¼ to one of four equal parts of this specific amount.
activities.rationale: A partitioned bar model makes the fraction-of-an-amount concrete and links it directly to division, targeting the common error of computing ¼ of £3.20 by an unclear operation. A live splittable bar lets the child act and see each equal part, but a drawn-and-divided paper bar serves the same purpose.
learnerActions: Take a bar representing £3.20 and split it into four equal parts.
Read what one part is worth and label it (80p / £0.80).
Write the matching calculation: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p.
Check by adding or multiplying back: 80p × 4 = £3.20.
State in your own words why 'a quarter of' means dividing by 4.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a fraction of an amount is a division: a quarter of £3.20 is £3.20 shared into 4 equal parts, which is 80p.

activities.title: Cut the rope: align the point before subtracting
feedback: If your answer is not 1.75 m, or does not match your ruler estimate, check whether 2.5 and 0.75 were lined up by their last digits instead of by the decimal point, and whether the exchange (borrowing) was done correctly.
Rewriting 2.5 as 2.50 does not change its value — it just makes the hundredths column visible for 0.75.
Compare your answer to the ruler: cutting a bit less than 1 m off 2.5 m should leave a bit more than 1.5 m and less than 2 m, so 1.75 m is sensible.
activities.rationale: The unequal lengths of 2.5 and 0.75 directly expose the misalignment error (right-justifying ragged decimals). A ruler or number line gives an independent size-check. Showing the aligned column subtraction makes the place-value structure explicit.
sourceClaims: Decimal errors in money and measurement contexts stem from whole-number thinking — reading the digits after the point as a separate whole number (the 'longer-is-larger' / whole-number-bias family) — rather than reasoning about each digit's place value; secure work requires place-value reasoning, not memorised digit rules.

KS2 money/measure problems require reading £3.20 as 3 pounds 20 pence (the tenths digit = 20p) and aligning decimal points when calculating; unit conversion (1 kg = 1000 g) links fractions, decimals and measures.
learnerActions: Start with a 2.5 m rope marked on a ruler or number line.
Cut off 0.75 m and predict the remaining length before calculating.
Rewrite 2.5 as 2.50 so both numbers have the same number of decimal places.
Stack 2.50 above 0.75 with the decimal points lined up vertically, then subtract with borrowing.
Read the remaining length (1.75 m) and check it against your prediction on the ruler.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals with different numbers of decimal places must be aligned on the decimal point before subtracting, because columns must match in place value; writing 2.5 as 2.50 is a helpful way to make the empty hundredths column visible.

activities.title: One mass, two notations: 3/10 of 1 kg
feedback: If 0.3 kg is converted to 30 g or 3000 g, recount the powers of ten: 3/10 of 1000 g is 300 g.
If only the grams (or only the decimal) were given, remember the question asks for both forms of the same mass.
A slider or double number line that lights up 300 g and 0.3 kg together shows they mark the same point.
activities.rationale: Converting both ways and expressing a single mass in two notations targets the unit-slip error and the half-answered question. The double number line keeps 1 kg = 1000 g visible as the anchor.
sourceClaims: KS2 money/measure problems require reading £3.20 as 3 pounds 20 pence (the tenths digit = 20p) and aligning decimal points when calculating; unit conversion (1 kg = 1000 g) links fractions, decimals and measures.
learnerActions: Anchor the fact 1 kg = 1000 g, e.g. on a double number line (kg on one side, g on the other).
Express the same mass as a decimal of a kilogram: 300 g = 0.3 kg.
Convert back the other way too: 0.3 kg = 300 g.
Explain why 300 g and 0.3 kg are two notations for the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: A quantity can be written as a fraction, as grams, or as a decimal of a kilogram, and converting fluently in both directions depends on anchoring 1 kg = 1000 g.

activities.title: Read the money by place value
feedback: If £3.20 is read as '3 pounds 2 pence', place coins: 2 tenths of a pound is two 10p coins = 20p.
If 2.5 m is read as '2 m and 5 cm', note that 5 tenths of a metre is 50 cm, since 1 m = 100 cm.
On the trap case, £3.5 is £3.50, because the 5 sits in the tenths place.
activities.rationale: This activity confronts the whole-number-bias misconception head-on by making the tenths digit concrete with coins and a ruler. The trap case is a diagnostic discrimination that is immediately resolved in favour of the place-value reading. Coins and a ruler are optional supports that make the tenth tangible; the reasoning is about place value, not the manipulative itself.
sourceClaims: Decimal errors in money and measurement contexts stem from whole-number thinking — reading the digits after the point as a separate whole number (the 'longer-is-larger' / whole-number-bias family) — rather than reasoning about each digit's place value; secure work requires place-value reasoning, not memorised digit rules.

KS2 money/measure problems require reading £3.20 as 3 pounds 20 pence (the tenths digit = 20p) and aligning decimal points when calculating; unit conversion (1 kg = 1000 g) links fractions, decimals and measures.
learnerActions: Look at £3.20 and say what each digit is worth: 3 pounds, 2 tenths of a pound, and 0 hundredths of a pound.
State what the 2 is worth in pence (20p, not 2p) and justify it.
Discuss the trap case: does £3.5 mean 3 pounds 5 pence or 3 pounds 50 pence? Explain which is correct and why.
Model an amount with coins and notes to confirm the tenths of a pound are 10p coins.
Repeat for a length: in 2.5 m, the 5 is 5 tenths of a metre = 50 cm, not 5 cm.
activities.intendedInsight: The digit after the decimal point is tenths of the unit, so the 2 in £3.20 is 20p and the 5 in £3.5 is 50p — not a separate whole number of the smaller unit.

activities.title: Quick checks on money, measure and conversion
feedback: 80p is correct because £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p; the 12.8p trap comes from treating £3.20 as the bare number 3.2 and multiplying (3.2 × 4 = 12.8) instead of dividing, and the 8p trap from dividing (3.2 ÷ 4 = 0.8) and misreading 0.8 of a pound as 8p rather than 80p.
For 2.50 − 0.75, align the points and exchange 1 one for 10 tenths: the answer is 1.75. A different result usually means the numbers were not lined up by the decimal point or the exchange went wrong.
0.3 kg = 300 g because 1 kg = 1000 g; 30 g or 3000 g uses the wrong power of ten.
activities.rationale: A short recognition/fill check consolidates the procedures and surfaces named error patterns. Recognition and fill-in-the-blank confirm answers but do not by themselves show independent construction of the method, so pairing them with a written step keeps the reasoning visible.
learnerActions: Answer: what is ¼ of £3.20? (Correct: 80p / £0.80. The traps 8p and 12.8p are wrong.)
Fill the blank: 2.50 − 0.75 = ___ m. (Correct: 1.75 m.)
Match 0.3 kg to its equivalent in grams (300 g).
For each, briefly write the step you used so the method is visible, not just the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: These calculations are cleanly checkable, and the wrong options correspond to specific errors (money-as-two-numbers, misalignment, unit slips) worth recognising and avoiding.

constraints: A static labelled shopping or measuring scene with tap-to-reveal can consolidate known facts and act as a reference, but it does not let the child perform the calculation, so it is a scaffold rather than the main activity.

Multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank items confirm correct answers and catch specific errors, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the method; ask the child to show steps.

Coins, notes, rulers, bar models and double number lines are optional supports that make tenths and conversions tangible; the target reasoning is place value and division, which can also be shown on paper.
Always require the child to show method (how they align the subtraction, how they divide for the fraction), not just the final number, because the method reveals the misconception.
Encourage estimating first to sense-check the size of each answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched this session. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One listed source (DfE national curriculum) is marked verified:false / not fetched this session in the original row; its claim is retained only where it directly supports a principle (reading £3.20 as 20p, point alignment, unit conversion), and its evidentiary strength is unconfirmed.

Independent self-audit of arithmetic: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p (80p × 4 = £3.20 ✓); the 12.8p trap = 3.2 × 4 (bare-number multiply) and the 8p trap = 3.2 ÷ 4 = 0.8 misread as 8p; 2.50 − 0.75 = 1.75 m ✓; 3/10 of 1 kg = 300 g = 0.3 kg ✓; £3.5 = £3.50 (tenths place) ✓. The 8p/12.8p attributions are consistent across activities 1 and 5.

The DfE source claim was removed from the fraction-of-an-amount activity, where it supported only the money topic and not the division principle; it remains where it directly supports reading £3.20 as 20p, point alignment, or unit conversion.

The £3.20-as-20p and £3.5-as-£3.50 prompts deliberately present the misconception as a discrimination to be explained, mirroring the original assessment's probing; each is immediately resolved in favour of the place-value reading in the feedback, so the wrong reading is never left standing as valid.

The original artefact-fit notes claimed depth 'adds nothing' for 3D and that in-role dialogue cannot deliver the insight; these are catalog preferences, not established facts, and have been dropped rather than asserted as universal laws.
The original suggestion to let the child mis-key '£3.20 = 302p' so a coin view corrects it is retained in spirit as an optional error-surfacing interaction, not as a required mechanism.

probeDeeper: In £3.20, what is the 2 worth — 2 pence or 20 pence? How do you know?
Why did you (or should you) write 2.5 as 2.50 before taking away 0.75?
How could you check that 80p really is a quarter of £3.20?
3/10 of 1 kg is 300 g — how do you write that as a decimal part of a kilogram, and why?

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a money or measure decimal as two whole numbers — '£3.20 is 3 pounds 2 pence', or 2.5 m is '2 m and 5 cm'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild place value: the 2 in £3.20 is 2 tenths of a pound = 20p; 0.5 m is 5 tenths of a metre = 50 cm. Use coins/ruler to make the tenth concrete.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the digit after the point as ones of the smaller unit regardless of place; ¼ of £3.20 comes out as pennies of '3.2', or 2.5 m handled as 2 m 5 cm

errorPatterns.pattern: Misaligns decimals of unequal length when subtracting — lines up 2.5 and 0.75 by their last digits instead of the point
errorPatterns.nextMove: Equalise lengths (2.50) and align on the decimal point, then subtract with borrowing exactly as for whole numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Does not rewrite 2.5 as 2.50; subtracts columns that don't match place value; answer like 1.85 or 2.25

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscomputes the fraction of an amount — ¼ of £3.20 by an unclear operation, not £3.20 ÷ 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect 'a quarter of' to dividing by 4 on the bar model; check 80p × 4 = £3.20.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: ¼ of £3.20 ≠ 80p; multiplies by 4, or takes 'a quarter' as 25 of something

errorPatterns.pattern: Unit-conversion slip — 0.3 kg given as 30 g or 3000 g, or grams found but not expressed as a decimal of a kg
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor 1 kg = 1000 g on a double number line; 3/10 of 1000 g = 300 g, and 300 g of 1000 is 0.3 kg.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Wrong power of ten in the kg→g conversion, or only half the question answered

responseLevels.gap: Reads money/measure decimals as two whole numbers and misaligns ragged subtractions; cannot reliably find a fraction of an amount or convert units.
responseLevels.full: Computes all three correctly with place-value reasoning — 80p as £3.20÷4, 1.75 m by aligned subtraction, 300 g = 0.3 kg both ways — estimates to check, and transfers to a new money/measure problem.
responseLevels.partial: Handles one or two parts correctly (e.g. ¼ of £3.20) but slips on the ragged subtraction or the unit conversion, or answers only part of the kilogram question.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Work these out and show your steps. First, what is 1/4 of £3.20? Second, a rope is 2.5 metres long and you cut off 0.75 metres — how much is left? Third, find 3/10 of 1 kilogram, and give the answer both in grams and as a decimal of a kilogram.' Watch the method — especially how they line up 2.5 and 0.75.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rope (2.5 − 0.75, unequal lengths) exposes decimal misalignment; the money reveals whether the child reads the 2 in £3.20 as 2 tenths of a pound (20p) or as 2 pence; the kilogram question checks unit fluency in both directions. A child who reads decimals as two whole numbers or right-justifies the subtraction gets the rope or the money wrong; a child reasoning by place value gets 80p, 1.75 m and 300 g / 0.3 kg.
